label: flagship: wins all three exams
result: Final results, all solutions replay-checked. The flagship setting allows two ordinary moves before planning. Standard exam (graded, 232 puzzles): 231 solved. The headline is a paired comparison against the plan language's own best. On the 225 puzzles where the exhaustive probe finished its search and the optimum is known, the best plan the language can express costs 0.98 extra moves and the flagship costs 0.76. The flagship is strictly shorter than that best plan on 27 of the 225 and strictly longer on 7. That limit binds any planner that speaks only that vocabulary. It is a measurement, not a mathematical proof. This change went below it. The unpaired figures are context only: 0.944 over the flagship's own 231 solves against the probe's 1.171 over the 228 puzzles it reaches. A third ordinary move improves the unpaired figure a little more, to 0.86 extra moves (average over its own 231 solves, the same solve count as the two-move version). Hard exam (frontier, 218 puzzles): 177 solved, needing about one fewer move than its matched control on the shared solves (47 wins, 2 losses). New-boards exam (unseen, 200 puzzles): 188 solved. 137 of the 200 carry a known optimum and the flagship solves 134 of those, with 1.47 extra moves vs perfect averaged over those 134. The win repeated with two different network pairs. It also worked, unchanged, on larger boards (17 wins, 0 losses on moves) and crowded boards (23 wins, 0 losses). Budget note, against the result: both arms run under a cap of 1200 expansions, but the hybrid's lanes add up to at most 1140 at depth 2 and 1160 at depth 3, so it wins while unable to reach the ceiling its control may use. Timing note: the two arms were never run at equal concurrency (control 8 instances wide with 2 threads each, hybrid 1 wide with 16), so no wall-clock claim is made. One caution: the rival move-by-move planner here is the original network. A re-tuned version would likely close part of the measured gap (see the project log, entry 24 — a companion document, not part of this page).
conclusion: Our flagship planner and the biggest finding of the program. Letting the planner make one or two ordinary moves before subgoal planning beats every pure-subgoal planner, everywhere we tried. A third move adds only a little. The benefit stops there.
note: Search-only change (no training); stochasticity is the search rng only. Gates: unseen moves 31/1 p=1.5e-8; graded moves 30/0 p=1.9e-9. Floor comparison paired over the 225 uncapped realizable rows with a known d* (probe 0.978 vs hybrid 0.760, 27 strictly shorter / 7 strictly longer); recomputed 2026-08-28, see FINDINGS 28.
